processing: Light to medium oxidation, semi-ball-rolled or strip-rolled in the Minnan style, finished with a light to medium roast; green and roasted versions both exist.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May) and autumn (October), plus summer pickings in the lower gardens; spring is the prized harvest.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly curved olive-green to brown semi-rolled leaves with pale tips and an orchid smell.
appearance_wet: Medium-sized, thick yellow-green leaves with reddish edges and whitish young tips.
taste_profile: Orchid over a sweet, honeyed, slightly creamy body with a gentle roast, a touch of Minnan briskness and a clean, lingering finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, then short steeps in a gaiwan; boiling water for roasted lots, a touch cooler for green ones. The orchid note is clearest in steeps two to four.

vintage_note: Sold by season, spring and autumn of the current year, in vacuum packs; lightly roasted lots are best within a year kept cool, roasted lots keep two to three years. Pinghe sellers increasingly state the village and the elevation; aged versions are uncommon.
description:
Bai Ya Qi Lan, white-bud rare orchid, is the signature tea of Pinghe county in the far south of Fujian, a semi-rolled oolong whose young shoots are a pale, whitish green and whose cup is all orchid and honey. The Wuyi Mountains also sell teas called Qi Lan, some of which may trace to this or related plants, but at home it is made in the lighter Minnan way.

The cultivar is a modern selection. It was picked out at Pengxi village in Pinghe's Qiling township from the local tea population, a single plant whose pale buds and orchid aroma stood out, by the county's tea station working with village technicians, and it was approved as a provincial cultivar in 1996; the whitish tips gave it the bai ya in its name and the orchid aroma the qi lan. Since then it has become Pinghe's main crop and the name is protected as a geographical indication.

In Pinghe it is oxidised lightly to moderately and rolled into semi-balls or loose curls rather than Anxi-style tight pellets, then given a light to medium roast; green-style lots exist too. The taste is orchid first, then a honeyed, slightly creamy sweetness, a gentle toast and a clean, cool finish, with a touch more briskness than Tieguanyin and less body than a Wuyi tea.

Brew it short and hot in a gaiwan and expect six or seven good infusions; the aroma peaks in the second to fourth steeps. It suits people who like the Tieguanyin family but want something less buttery and a little more roasted.

It is sold by season, spring and autumn, and should be drunk fresh, within a year for green lots and two or three for roasted ones. The county has high gardens on Daqin Mountain and lower, warmer ones, and sellers increasingly name the village and elevation; higher lots are more fragrant and cost more. For a contrast in place and roast, compare it with a Wuyi Qi Lan.
history:
Bai Ya Qi Lan belongs to Pinghe county in the south of Fujian, grown mainly around Qiling and Jiufeng at the foot of Daqin Mountain; Pengxi village in Qiling is named as its home. It is a modern selection, not an old tea. The county agriculture bureau's tea station and technicians from Pengxi picked out a single plant from the local tea population.

The cultivar passed provincial approval in 1996, and in September 2002 it received origin-trademark registration from the national quality inspection authority. It now counts as a Chinese geographical indication product. The year of the original selection did not turn up in the sources read here.
